we have investigated the roles of photo-carriers and driving wavelength on high harmonic generation (HHG) from semiconducting crystals, and demonstrated the possibility to identify and control the dominant mechanism of HHG from semiconductives.
we have demonstrated a distinct control of the high harmonic generation from semiconducting materials, and have revealed the underlying mechanism of the harmonic generation process.

the photo-carrier doping in a semiconductor and the wavelength of driving field can be used to control the harmonic properties, and the harmonic spectra from the semiconductor can be used to distinguish the contributions from the interband and intrasubband transitions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the generation of high harmonics in semiconductors.
the generation of high harmonics from a semiconductor.
the generation mechanism of high harmonics from solids, and the control over the harmonic properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the photo-carriers are injected into the conduction and valence bands of semiconductors.

the harmonic emission from semiconducting materials is a complex process that is affected by a number of parameters, including the carrier density, the carrier lifetime, the band structure of the material, the driving wavelength, the driving pulse duration and intensity and the harmonic wavelength.
the interband and intrasubband contributions to high harmonic generation in semiconductors have been identified, and their relative contributions can be controlled through the photo-carrier density.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we demonstrate a new method to control high harmonic generation from semiconducting solids, and the method can also be applied to control high harmonics from gas phase.
the harmonic process in a semiconductor can be controlled by adjusting the driving wavelength and the photo-carrier density.
high harmonics from solids can be manipulated by controlling the photo-carriers, and the harmonic properties depend on the wavelength of the driving laser.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the harmonic spectra from semiconducting materials are highly dependent on the photo-carrier density, which is a unique property absent in the case of gas-phase media.
we can control the harmonic process from a semiconductor by changing the photo-carrier density and driving wavelengths.
